满眼游丝兼落絮，红杏开时，一霎清明雨。

4月这波行情，大概就是这种感觉。

前一秒还春风得意，后一秒就黑云压城。

BTC 刚冲起来，宏观消息一落，市场立刻翻脸。  

熬夜盯盘、频繁做短的人，应该都懂这种窒息感：

你以为自己在抓机会，其实大多数时候，是在给波动交学费。

我也是这么被教育过来的。

那段时间天天盯盘，短线没做明白，头发先掉了，本金也越磨越薄。  

爆仓那晚，我想明白一件事打不过，就别硬打。

于是我开始在 @Bybit_Official 上研究跟单。

但实盘交了几千U学费后，我发现：

很多人不是不会跟单，是一开始就把跟单这件事理解错了。

如果你只是按收益率排行榜选人，  
那不是跟单。是去给别人当燃料。

我后来复盘，真正最坑人的，不是方向错了。  
而是你跟了一个看起来很稳的人。

尤其是那种：

- 胜率特别高
- 曲线特别顺
- 最近收益特别炸

刚开始我也信过。

结果一波急跌下来，对方死扛不止损，前面所有漂亮数据瞬间失真。

后来我才看明白：

很多高胜率，本质上是小赚就跑，亏损死扛

只要亏损单一直不平，账面胜率就能一直好看。

震荡市里甚至真能做出百战百胜的假象。  

可一旦遇到单边行情，先蒸发的往往不是他，是你。

所以现在我选带单员，不先看收益。

第一，看最大回撤。  
这是最真实的底色。

收益可以包装，胜率可以修饰，回撤骗不了人。

我的标准

30天最大回撤超过20%，直接拉黑。

因为这意味着他不是在稳定交易，  
而是在拿未来的风险换现在的数据。

第二，看稳定性。  
我现在越来越不信短期翻倍。

市场最不缺的，就是一时风光的人。  
真正稀缺的是：

- 波动可控
- 曲线稳定
- 能穿越剧烈行情
- 能长期留在牌桌上

第三，看风险收益比。  

同样是赚钱，有的人靠系统，有的人靠赌命。

前者能复利，后者迟早归零。

但说到底，选对人也只是一半。

另一半，在你自己手里。

很多人以为找到一个厉害的带单员，后面就可以躺平。  

真正决定你能不能活下来的，是你自己的参数设置。

我现在最重视两件事：

一是用进阶跟单，把风险锁死。  
尤其是自定义保证金、杠杆上限。

你永远不知道带单员下一笔会不会突然上头。但你可以提前把自己的风险封顶。

这是防火墙。

二是一定要设追踪止损。  
币圈里很多利润，最后都不是亏在没赚到，是亏在赚到了却没带走。

我的习惯是，只要账户利润拉起来，就把退出线提前写死。

这样做很简单：

- 行情继续走，我继续拿
- 行情一反转，我自动撤

利润没落袋之前，都不算真正属于你。

一键跟单从来不是什么暴富魔法。
它本质上是投资组合管理。

带单员负责冲锋。  
你自己，必须负责风控。

用数据筛掉伪神。  
用参数锁死底线。  
用规则保住利润。

市场最终尊重的，从来不是最激进的人。

而是最清醒的人。

So you keep getting faked out on trades and don't know why?

Probably because you don't understand Breakout trading yet

Sounds complicated? It's not. Here's the quick breakdown:

What is a breakout?

When price pushes through a key support or resistance level with momentum. It signals a shift in power between buyers and sellers, and that's where the opportunity lives

Two types you need to know:

Bullish breakout - price breaks ABOVE resistance, buyers are in control, you go long

Bearish breakout - price breaks BELOW support, sellers took over, you go short

How to trade it:

1. Mark your key support and resistance levels on the chart

2. Wait for price to approach these levels (patience is everything here)

3. Confirm the breakout with volume - no volume = no conviction = likely a fake move

4. Enter in the direction of the break

5. Set your stop-loss just below the breakout level (bullish) or just above it (bearish)

6. Target a >2:1 reward-to-risk ratio

What triggers breakouts?

News and announcements - partnerships, regulations, macro events

Sentiment shifts - FOMO and fear move markets faster than fundamentals

Technical patterns - triangles, flags, head-and-shoulders all set up breakouts

Indicators that help confirm:

RSI - above 70 signals overbought, below 30 signals oversold

Moving Average crossovers - short-term crossing long-term confirms direction

Volume - the single most important confirmation tool. High volume = real breakout

Pro Tip: The #1 mistake beginners make is jumping in too early. False breakouts will destroy your account if you don't wait for confirmation. Let the candle CLOSE beyond the level before you enter. And never risk more than 1-2% of your capital on a single trade

Being able to pay gas fees with $BTC on Cardano might not seem like a big deal at first, but compared to other chains, the approach is fundamentally different.

If you look at Ethereum, paying gas with tokens usually involves something like a paymaster contract. That means the dApp has to integrate specific contracts and infrastructure to support it. 

This adds complexity, creates dependencies on certain implementations, and introduces potential risks like contract vulnerabilities or funds being exposed. Most chains handle token-based gas payments this way.

Cardano, on the other hand, is designed to support this at the protocol level through mechanisms like Babel fees. There’s no need to deploy special contracts or integrate additional infrastructure. It can handled at the tx construction stage, and you can pay fees in tokens other than $ADA without relying on specific operators or contracts.

As a result, Bitcoin holders could potentially pay gas in $BTC on Cardano, without needing to hold or top up $ADA, and manage their assets in a much more seamless way.

Take it a step further, and BTC holders might end up using DeFi on Cardano without even realizing it, that’s how seamless the UX could get.

This isn’t just a feature difference. It’s a fundamentally different design approach. I think this is one of the reasons why Cardano is well suited for Bitcoin DeFi.

Heinz estimates the lifetime value of a ketchup customer at ~$1000 ($50/year).

Starbucks is ~$14000; Netflix $290; McDonald’s $5000.

Other than at MegaETH, I’ve rarely heard of a crypto project even attempting to estimate this number for themselves.

Same for cost of customer acquisition.

I think this reflects a low level of curiosity about user base. But perhaps more importantly, it reflects a lack of thinking on the margin.

You always want to be thinking in terms of the NEXT user, dollar of TVL, or transaction.

Consider a DEX with $50m of LPing capital. When designing an incentives program, this DEX cares about attracting new LPers.

Where possible, it is likely best to design incentives such that they are concentrated on new liquidity provision, since the existing $50m is already willing to LP on the basis of existing yield.

This introduces complexity, because the DEX now needs to track the marginal LP increase, and also avoid incentivizing existing LPs from withdrawing and re-entering to capture a windfall yield.

It’s hard, so most projects just throw a yield on top, which ends up targeting the average liquidity provider, rather than the marginal one.

That overpays LPs who were already willing to show up, and leave less money available to pay more yield-sensitive LPs.

Net result is less marginal growth for the same budget. 

Interestingly, this is the textbook pricing model of monopolists. The difference is the monopolist captures monopoly profits from this pricing system, while a crypto project bears the cost of the inefficiency itself.

I think a lot of the complaints around incentives programs have their roots in this accidental targeting of average (rather than marginal) user acquisition cost, lifetime value, etc. That in turn seems to stem from a profound lack of curiosity about who relevant stakeholders are, what their needs are, and how to attract one more of them.

Unfortunately, it’s easier said than done to figure this out.

Bitcoin has never been hacked, not even once in more than 15 years.

What people usually call Bitcoin hacks were not attacks on the Bitcoin blockchain itself. They were attacks on exchanges that are companies built on top of Bitcoin that hold customer funds, that distinction matters.

The blockchain is the protocol while
Exchanges are businesses.
Protocols run on math and consensus, and businesses run on people, systems and security practices.

Here are some of the biggest exchange failures in crypto history and figures are stipulated based on year attacked:

-Bybit lost $1.46B (Feb 2025)
Around 401,000 ETH was drained from multisig wallets within minutes. Investigators linked the attack to North Korean hackers. It became one of the largest financial thefts ever recorded.

-Coincheck lost  $534M (Jan 2018)
A major Japanese exchange lost over half a billion dollars after private keys were compromised.

-Mt. Gox lost $470M (2011–2014)
The most infamous case. Rather than a single breach, funds were reportedly drained over years. About 850,000 BTC disappeared. At its peak, Mt. Gox handled roughly 70% of global Bitcoin trading volume. It filed for bankruptcy in 2014 a sad end.

- FTX lost $415M (Nov 2022)
Funds were stolen the same night the exchange collapsed into bankruptcy. The scandal later led to criminal convictions of senior leadership, the popular Sam Bankman-Fried jail.

-DMM Bitcoin lost $305M (May 2024)
Over 4,500 BTC was stolen in a major breach. The exchange later announced plans to shut down.

-WazirX lost $234M (Jul 2024)
India’s largest exchange at the time suffered a multisig wallet exploit that wiped out a significant portion of assets.

-Bitfinex lost $72M (Aug 2016)
About 120,000 BTC was stolen. Years later U.S. authorities recovered much of it.

Across nearly every case, the issue was not Bitcoin itself it was:
- Poor private key security
-Weak internal controls
-Custodial risk
-Overreliance on trusted third parties
-Human error

Bitcoin’s blockchain kept producing blocks exactly as designed while the companies holding customer coins did not.

The lesson here is that if someone else controls your keys they control your money.

Not your keys, not your coins. Stay safu.
